The Swedish of the future: what English, TikTok and new generations are doing to it

Languages are often described as if they were standing in a museum. There are correct words, correct rules and people who protect it all from being “spoiled”.

But Swedish isn’t standing still. It swaps messages in chats, changes in multilingual neighbourhoods, borrows English verbs and regularly argues with itself about what has already become the norm.

English word, Swedish grammar

A borrowing doesn’t always enter a language in its original form. Swedish can take an English stem and add its own grammar.

For example, in conversation you can come across verbs formed from English words but conjugated according to the Swedish pattern. This shows something important: the word is no longer just a guest. It starts to live by the rules of the new language.

Such forms can annoy supporters of linguistic purity, but for younger speakers they can feel completely natural.

Chats shorten more than just words

In messages, capital letters, punctuation and some formal greetings disappear. Emojis can stand in for the tone that intonation would carry in speech.

Compare:

Hej! Skulle du kunna skicka bilden när du har tid? Tack!

and

kan du skicka bilden sen? 🙏

The second phrase is shorter, but the emoji softens the request. Without it, the same text can seem more abrupt – depending on the relationship.

Typ, ba and asså

Young people’s speech and informal speech have a rhythm of their own.

  • typ signals approximation or works as a filler;
  • ba, related to bara, often introduces a reaction or a remark;
  • asså, from alltså, can mark an explanation, surprise or an emotional lead-in.
Och jag ba: va?

And I was like: what?

This isn’t a phrase to put in a formal letter. But if you’ve never heard it, part of a TV series or a conversation between teenagers may be lost on you.

Hen and a language looking for new solutions

Alongside han and hon, modern Swedish uses the gender-neutral pronoun hen. It can be appropriate when a person’s gender is unknown or unimportant, or when the person themselves uses this pronoun.

A new word may at first provoke heated debate and then become an ordinary tool. That is how a language responds to new communication needs.

Multilingual Sweden creates Swedish too

Modern Swedish is shaped not only by English and the internet. People with different first languages speak it every day. Their children grow up with Swedish, but bring a different rhythm, vocabulary and cultural references to it.

Urban youth varieties can’t be reduced to “bad Swedish”. They have social functions of their own: they show belonging, closeness, humour and the speaker’s stance.

At the same time, it’s important for a student to distinguish between:

  • what you need to understand;
  • what you can use with friends;
  • what is appropriate at work;
  • what is best kept for the specific group you truly belong to.

Do you need to learn all the new slang?

No. Slang changes quickly, and trying to sound “very youthful” sometimes has the opposite effect.

A more useful strategy:

  1. First, learn to recognise the word.
  2. See who uses it, and in which situations.
  3. Don’t automatically carry it over into formal speech.
  4. Use only what naturally suits your age, environment and style.

Who decides what is correct

Dictionaries, language institutions, newsrooms and schools describe the language and set its norms. But change starts with speakers. If a new form spreads, becomes established and fills a real need, indignation alone can no longer undo it.

This doesn’t mean there are no rules any more. It means that the rules depend on context. What works brilliantly on TikTok can be inappropriate in an application to an official body – and vice versa.

Try it yourself

Match the forms to the situations: a chat with a friend, a message to a colleague, a formal letter.

  • Tja! Kan du skicka den sen?
  • Hej! Kan du skicka dokumentet när du har möjlighet?
  • Hej, jag skulle vilja be er att skicka dokumentet till följande adress.

All three can be correct. It’s not only a matter of grammar, but of relationships and purpose.

Do anglicisms spoil Swedish?

Borrowings change a language, but language contact has always existed. Whether a particular word is appropriate depends on the context.

Should a beginner learn slang?

You don’t have to use it actively. But gradually learning to recognise common spoken forms is very useful for listening comprehension.
